rv.q: Richard Eyre’s revival, which began life in Bristol and now comes into London with the Tyrone sons recast, is shatteringly good.
Her performance is a tour de force.
It's a staggering performance. Manville makes Mary the unsteady linchpin of Eugene O'Neill's unwieldy masterpiece.
In Richard Eyre's painfully intense production, these troubled figures are resurrected with both unsparing naturalism and just enough tenderness to make their flaws all the more painful.

It’s a welcome touch of light relief in a play that if well done, as it is here, leaves you emotionally pulverised by the feeling that O’Neill, in providing an unsparing portrait of his family, is seeking their posthumous forgiveness.
It remains a gruelling experience — Eyre calls it 'the saddest play ever written' — but has a naked emotional power that's genuinely absorbing.
Eyre’s production makes it easy to see why.
The evening attains the immense poignancy that explains the play’s enduring status.
This is a performance of detailed genius and for all the excellence surrounding her, she makes it her play.
Manville provides the ecstatic charge in it.
Sad to say, though, Irons disappoints.

cn.t: Eyre's production of O'Neill's masterpiece earns mostly strong praise for Manville and Irons' powerful performances and its raw emotional intensity, though a few critics find the three-and-a-half-hour family drama grueling and overrated.
